in_text_mentions: tation measures. The newborn was admitted to the neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) at birth for three days due to unexplained hypoglycemia. One week later, he experienced another NICU admission lasting 21 days due to late-onset sepsis. During this period, he developed erythematous, tender plaques on the back and shoulders, and multiple red nodules on the posterior aspects of the legs (Figure 1). Ultrasound (US) examination of the skin lesions revealed multifocal thickening of the subcutaneous tissue with no evident underlying cystic or solid lesions, thereby supporting the diagnosis of SFNN.

panels.rationale: Single-panel low-power H&E skin biopsy from a newborn (article title: Subcutaneous Fat Necrosis of the Newborn After Whole-Body Cooling for Birth Asphyxia). The caption and in-text describe superficial fat lobules that are intact with well-preserved adipocytes (black arrow) contrasting with deeper fat showing collapsed morphology, loss of distinct cell borders and necrosis (white arrows), and the in-text explicitly states these features indicated lobular panniculitis for Figures 2 and 3. This is a real human-patient histopathology image showing a specific manifestation of subcutaneous fat necrosis of the newborn; no third-party copyright, no diagram/chart, and no other disease. Arrows are present as annotations. No needle-shaped clefts are clearly identifiable at this low power and they are not mentioned for this figure, so that finding is not tagged.

The disease-focused article title ('Early Recognition of Subcutaneous Fat Necrosis of the Newborn With Atypical Purpuric Presentation') together with the in-text statement that the firm violaceous plaque on the upper back was the SCFN lesion and that dermoscopic evaluation of that same lesion revealed a central dark reddish-purpuric zone with an irregular serrated erythematous margin, vascular disruption and peripheral pallor establishes SCFN attribution. The caption explicitly states these features are not typically described in SCFN, so the presentation is tagged atypical. The only vocabulary finding applicable is the indurated erythematous/violaceous plaque (supported by the in-text 'firm, violaceous plaque'); the specific dermoscopic descriptors are not in the vocabulary and are listed as proposed findings. Body site (upper back) and neonate status (day three of life) come from the in-text mention. No ethnicity is stated. Skin in the adequately lit periphery appears light (Fitzpatrick I-II). No arrows, labels or other annotations are present.

panels.rationale: Single clinical photograph from a case report titled 'Radiologic Evaluation of Subcutaneous Fat Necrosis Complicated by an Abscess in a Newborn' showing a raised erythematous/violaceous indurated plaque with swelling on day of life 11, a textbook cutaneous presentation of subcutaneous fat necrosis of the newborn.
panels.attribution_text: Al-Kharabsheh et al. Radiologic Evaluation of Subcutaneous Fat Necrosis Complicated by an Abscess in a Newborn: A Case Report.. Cureus 2025. doi:10.7759/cureus.87247. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 4.
panels.figure_caption: Increased fluctuance and swelling on DOL 11 DOL: day of life
in_text_mentions: On DOL 11, the erythema showed slight improvement, but fluctuance and swelling continued to evolve (Figure 4). Serum calcium and ionized calcium levels on DOL 12 increased to 11.5 mg/dL and 1.32 mmol/L (normal, 1.12-1.30), respectively. A follow-up ultrasound demonstrated continued diffuse echogenic thickening of the subcutaneous tissues (4.9 × 4.2 × 0.9 cm) (Figures 5, 6). The imaging findings were considered most consistent with subcutaneous fat necrosis of the newborn; however, cellulitis remained within the differential diagnosis, as it is similar in appearance on US imaging.
